newsitem.title: USA: General Mills must permit Chex competition.
newsitem.headline: General Mills must permit Chex competition.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission acted Thursday to prevent a corporate purchase from driving up the price of Chex brand cereals, the FTC announced.
The FTC voted, 3-2, that General Mills could purchase Chex branded cereals from Ralcorp Holdings only if it permitted unfettered competition by private brands through Ralcorp's "New Ralcorp" entity.

"Conditions attached to clearing the merger are designed to eliminate fully and immediately any barriers to New Ralcorp competing aggressively in promoting private label products," said FTC Chairman Robert Pitofsky in a statement.

General Mills purchased the name-brand cereals business of Ralcorp in a deal worth $570 million. As part of the deal, Ralcorp agreed to wait 18 months before selling Chex cereals through private labels, which appear under store or wholesaler names.
In addition, General Mills would have to give permission before New Ralcorp could allow anyone else to manufacture and sell private label cereals identical to Chex products.
The FTC said neither of those restrictions could stand because they would have set barriers to others trying to compete, resulting in higher prices on Chex cereals.
Commissioner Roscoe Starek dissented. He said consumers have many alternatives if a breakfast cereal producer raises prices. He said it was "completely unnecessary" to have the FTC agreement.
Commissioner Mary Azcuenaga dissented in part, opposing elimination of the 18-month noncompetitive clause in the merger.
General Mills, based in Minneapolis, Minn., agreed to the conditions to acquire the name-brand breakfast cereal and snack mix business of Ralcorp, based in St. Louis, Mo.
Ralcorp was created by Ralston Purina Co. in 1994 to license Ralston Purina technology.

The FTC had said General Mills' acquisition of the branded cereal business of Ralcorp would boost its share of the U.S. breakfast cereal market to 31 percent. The FTC said it had sales of $2.75 billion in fiscal 1996 of ready-to-eat cereals.
The largest producer of such cereals is Kellogg Co.
